entries.question: What's new?
entries.summary: Ecclesiastes 1:9 says nothing is new under the sun and nothing ever will be. Isaiah 43:19 and 65:17, 2 Corinthians 5:17, 2 Peter 3:13, and Revelation 21:1 all announce that God is making new things, new creations, new heavens, and a new earth. The Qohelet-Stoic cyclical worldview and the apocalyptic-eschatological new-creation worldview run on opposite metaphysics.
entries.commentary:
Qohelet's 1:9 — 'there is nothing new under the sun' (ein kol chadash tachat hashemesh) — is the doctrinal anchor of the whole book's cyclical pessimism. Choon-Leong Seow in the AB Ecclesiastes volume reads this as classic Hellenistic-era resignation literature: the world runs in repeating loops, history doesn't progress, what looks novel is just the same patterns recombining. Longman in the NICOT puts it bluntly: Qohelet's worldview is anti-eschatological. There is no breakthrough coming, no rupture, no new thing.

Isaiah 43:19 and 65:17 say exactly the opposite. Hineni oseh chadashah — 'behold, I am doing a new thing' — is Second Isaiah's announcement of a coming intervention so categorically novel that the old categories won't survive. Joseph Blenkinsopp in the AB Isaiah 40-55 volume documents how the chadash language in Deutero-Isaiah is deliberately polemical against ancient Near Eastern cyclical cosmology — YHWH disrupts cycles. Third Isaiah's 65:17 escalates this to cosmic scale: new heavens and a new earth, with the old ones not even remembered. Blenkinsopp's AB Isaiah 56-66 reads this as proto-apocalyptic — the seedbed of the genre that Revelation will later inherit.

The New Testament rolls in the same direction. Victor Paul Furnish in the AB II Corinthians reads 2 Cor 5:17 — kaine ktisis, new creation — as Paul's most condensed statement of inaugurated eschatology. Richard Bauckham in the WBC 2 Peter and David Aune in the WBC Revelation 17-22 trace the Isaianic new-heavens-new-earth language straight into the apocalyptic finale. The eschatological strand of the Bible is built on the premise that newness is precisely what God specializes in.

The apologist response usually runs: Qohelet was speaking of nothing new under the natural order, while the prophets speak of supernatural new acts of God. Tremper Longman makes a version of this move, and to be fair, it's a plausible reading — 'under the sun' could be a register-restriction. But the harmonization doesn't survive contact with the actual texts. Qohelet 1:9 frames its claim universally — kol chadash, 'any new thing' — and the cyclical examples in 1:5-7 are cosmic, not merely sublunar. Qohelet is denying eschatology as a category. The apocalyptic strand depends on the category Qohelet denies. The contradiction is between two competing Jewish theologies of time: one wisdom-Hellenistic and cyclical, the other prophetic-apocalyptic and rupturalist. The Bible contains both, and they don't agree.

answers.answer: Nothing is, or ever will be, new.
answers.answer_explanation: There is nothing new under the sun. Ecclesiastes 1:9

Behold, I will do a new thing. Isaiah 43:19
				
				        For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth. Isaiah 65:17
				
				    


				     Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are
				    passed away; behold, all things are become new. 2 Corinthians 5:17
				
				        Nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth. 2 Peter 3:13
				
				        
And I saw a new heaven and a new earth. Revelation 21:1

commentary_out.commentary:
Qohelet's thesis statement in 1:9 — *ʾeyn kol-ḥadash taḥat ha-shemesh*, "there is nothing new under the sun" — is the doctrinal anchor of the book's cyclical pessimism, and the surrounding verses (1:4-7) supply the cosmology that makes the claim work: generations come and go, the sun rises and sets and hurries back, the wind circles, the rivers run to a sea that is never full. The governing image is the loop. Choon-Leong Seow, in the Anchor Bible Ecclesiastes, reads it as resignation literature: history does not progress, and what looks novel is merely the recombination of established patterns. On the dating, Seow is the standard-bearer for the minority view — he places Qohelet in the Persian period (second half of the fifth to first half of the fourth century BCE) on the strength of Persian loanwords, dense Aramaisms, and administrative vocabulary, and he resists reading the book as a response to Greek philosophy. The critical majority still dates it later, to the Hellenistic third century, but that consensus is theirs, not Seow's. Tremper Longman, in the NICOT volume, states the implication plainly — Qohelet's worldview is anti-eschatological. There is no coming rupture, no breakthrough, no genuinely new thing. As a thematic parallel and not a dating argument, the closest analogue is the Greek conception of cyclical time — the *anakyklōsis* of Polybius, the recurrence motifs of Stoic cosmology — and while direct dependence is unprovable, the resonance is real and tells against reading 1:9 as a narrowly empirical remark.

Second Isaiah says the opposite, and says it programmatically. *Hineni ʿoseh ḥadashah* — "behold, I am doing a new thing" (43:19) — is the announcement of an intervention so categorically novel that the old categories will not survive it. Joseph Blenkinsopp, in the Anchor Bible Isaiah 40-55, documents how the *ḥadash* vocabulary in Deutero-Isaiah is deliberately polemical against Babylonian and broader ancient Near Eastern cyclical cosmology: YHWH is the one who disrupts the cycle, who makes a way in the wilderness where there was none. Third Isaiah escalates the claim to cosmic scale in 65:17 — "new heavens and a new earth" so total that "the former things shall not be remembered." Blenkinsopp's companion volume on Isaiah 56-66 reads this as proto-apocalyptic, the seedbed of the genre Revelation later inherits. The New Testament runs the same direction: Victor Paul Furnish reads 2 Cor 5:17's *kainē ktisis* ("new creation") as Paul's most condensed statement of inaugurated eschatology, and Richard Bauckham (on 2 Peter) and David Aune (on Revelation) trace the Isaianic new-heavens-new-earth language straight into the apocalyptic finale. The whole eschatological strand is built on the premise that newness is precisely what God specializes in. John Collins's survey of the apocalyptic imagination underscores how alien this rupturalist metaphysic is to the sapiential outlook.

The standard harmonization — articulated in various forms by Longman and by apologetic commentators — restricts Qohelet's scope: "under the sun" (*taḥat ha-shemesh*) marks a register, the sublunar natural order observed without revelation, so that Qohelet denies novelty in nature while the prophets announce supernatural new acts of God. This deserves a fair hearing, because "under the sun" is in fact Qohelet's signature qualifier (it recurs roughly thirty times across the book, depending on how one counts), and one can read it as bracketing the divine vantage. But the harmonization does not survive contact with the text's own phrasing. The claim of 1:9 is universal — *kol ḥadash*, "any new thing" — and the supporting examples in 1:5-7 are cosmic (sun, wind, sea), not narrowly terrestrial. Qohelet is not carving out a domain in which God might still innovate; he is denying eschatology as a category of expectation. The apocalyptic strand depends on exactly the category Qohelet rejects. The deeper point is that this is not a clumsy author contradicting himself but two competing Jewish theologies of time housed in one canon: a wisdom-Hellenistic outlook that is cyclical and a prophetic-apocalyptic outlook that is rupturalist. The redaction-critical history matters here — Qohelet is late (Persian period, late fifth to early fourth century BCE, on Seow's dating; the third century on the majority view), and the new-creation eschatology of Trito-Isaiah and the apocalypses crystallizes alongside and after it, so the canon preserves a live intramural dispute rather than a settled doctrine. Verdict: genuine theological contradiction; the register-restriction reading softens but cannot dissolve a claim the text frames universally.

commentary_out.change_summary: Doubled the commentary with Hebrew detail on the cyclical formulas, Stoic/ANE comparative parallels, the redactional layering of Isaiah, the genre frame of Qohelet, and a fuller weighing of the 'under the sun' register-restriction argument. Audit fixes: corrected the garbled Hebrew transliteration of Eccl 1:9 from 'taḥat ha-shamesh' to the proper 'taḥat ha-shemesh' (תַּחַת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ); replaced the false-precision claim that 'under the sun' recurs 'some twenty-nine times' with the hedged 'roughly thirty times across the book, depending on how one counts.' Pass-3 medium fix: corrected the misattribution of Qohelet's dating to Seow — Seow is in fact the leading proponent of the PERSIAN-period dating (late 5th to early 4th c. BCE, on Persian loanwords/Aramaisms), arguing against the Hellenistic consensus, so the commentary now credits the Persian-period dating to Seow and assigns the third-century/Hellenistic dating to the critical majority instead. The Stoic/Hellenistic resonance is retained explicitly as a thematic parallel only, not hung on Seow's dating. The 'roughly thirty times' hedge is left as-is per the auditor's own note that it requires no change.

issues.problem: Misattributes a dating/positioning to Choon-Leong Seow that is the opposite of his published view. The commentary says Seow 'situates this within Hellenistic-era Jewish wisdom,' and the change_summary parenthetical asserts 'Qohelet is late (third century BCE on Seow's dating).' Seow is in fact the scholar best known for arguing AGAINST the Hellenistic/third-century dating: in the Anchor Bible Ecclesiastes (18C) he dates Qohelet to the Persian period (roughly the second half of the 5th to the first half of the 4th century BCE) on the basis of Persian loanwords, Aramaisms, and economic-vocabulary evidence, and explicitly resists reading it as interacting with Greek philosophy. Attributing the majority Hellenistic dating to Seow is a factual misattribution of a named scholar's position.
issues.correction: Replace 'Hellenistic-era Jewish wisdom' framing of Seow with his actual Persian-period dating, and change 'third century BCE on Seow's dating' to Seow's late-Persian-period dating (late 5th-early 4th c. BCE); alternatively attribute the third-century/Hellenistic dating to the majority of critical scholars (not to Seow specifically). The Stoic/Hellenistic comparative resonance argued elsewhere in the paragraph is fine as a thematic parallel but must not be hung on Seow's dating.

issues.problem: Minor: 'roughly thirty times across the book, depending on how one counts' for the 'under the sun' formula. Standard counts give 29 occurrences of tachat hashemesh; 'roughly thirty' is an acceptable hedge. entries.question: What was Sodom's sin?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Leviticus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Wisdom, Matthew, Luke, 2 Peter, Jude
entries.summary: The Bible names at least six different sins as the reason Sodom was destroyed: same-sex intercourse (Leviticus 18:22 read into Ezekiel 16:50), inhospitality (Matthew 10, Luke 10, Wisdom 19:13), seeking sex with angels and 'strange flesh' (Genesis 19, Jude 7), pride and neglect of the poor (Isaiah 1, Ezekiel 16:49), adultery and lying (Jeremiah 23:14), and generic ungodliness (2 Peter 2). The 'homosexuality' reading is a late interpretive overlay that the Hebrew Bible's own internal cross-references don't support.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest examples in the canon of an interpretive trajectory overwriting the source text. Genesis 19 records a mob demanding to 'know' (yada) two angelic visitors at Lot's house. The verb yada in Hebrew has a sexual sense in a minority of its 943 occurrences, but the demand context here makes a sexual reading defensible. What the verb does not specify is that the sin is the same-sex orientation of the act rather than the gang-rape-of-foreigners structure of it. Susan Niditch in *Judges* (OTL) and Phyllis Trible in *Texts of Terror* both document how the Genesis 19 / Judges 19 parallel — the Gibeah outrage — is structurally about violation of guest-rights through sexual violence, not about same-sex desire as such.

More decisively: when the Hebrew Bible looks back at Sodom, it does not name same-sex intercourse. Ezekiel 16:49 lists Sodom's iniquity in order — pride, surfeit of bread, prosperous ease, failure to aid the poor and needy. Walther Zimmerli in the Hermeneia Ezekiel 1 commentary takes this list at face value: the prophetic indictment of Sodom is socioeconomic and theological, not sexual in the modern sense. Verse 50 adds 'they did toevah before me' — and toevah is a wide-spectrum abomination term that the apologist crowd reads as referring to Leviticus 18:22, but which Zimmerli notes more naturally refers to the cumulative arrogance just listed. Isaiah 1:10-17 makes the same point with the same emphasis: the 'rulers of Sodom' are corrupt judges who oppress the widow and the orphan. Jeremiah 23:14 cites Sodom for adultery and lying among the prophets. The OT trajectory is consistent and it isn't about homosexuality.

The Synoptic Jesus follows that trajectory. Matthew 10:14-15 and Luke 10:10-12 cite Sodom as the type-case of inhospitality — the rejection of God's messengers — and Wisdom 19:13-17, written in Greek-speaking Jewish Alexandria, makes this completely explicit: Sodom's sin was that they 'practiced a more bitter hatred of strangers.' That's the inherited interpretation through at least the first century CE.

The shift happens with Jude 7's 'strange flesh' (sarkos heteras) and the Second Temple para-biblical literature — 1 Enoch 6-11, Jubilees 16, the Testament of Naphtali — where Sodom gets read through the Watchers-Genesis 6 lens of human-angel sexual transgression. Richard Bauckham in the WBC Jude / 2 Peter documents this trajectory with care. The Jude reading is angelic-sex transgression, not human same-sex orientation. The further shift to 'homosexuality' is a medieval and early modern Christian retrojection, securely placed by John Boswell in *Christianity, Social Tolerance, and Homosexuality* and more recently by Bernadette Brooten in *Love Between Women*.

The critical reading is straightforward: Sodom's sin in the Hebrew Bible and its first-century inheritors is pride, social oppression, and inhospitality; in the Second Temple apocalyptic tradition it expands to include forbidden angel-flesh crossing; the modern 'homosexuality' reading is anachronistic. The SAB framing as 'contradiction' is correct on the surface but undersells the more interesting point — the biblical authors knew what Sodom's sin was, and it wasn't what twentieth-century preachers said it was.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest cases in the canon of an interpretive trajectory overwriting its source text. Genesis 19 records a mob demanding to "know" (*yadaʿ*) two angelic visitors at Lot's house. The verb *yadaʿ* carries a sexual sense in only a small minority of its occurrences in the Hebrew Bible, but the demand-context here, together with Lot's counter-offer of his daughters, makes a sexual reading of the mob's intent defensible. What the verb does not specify is that the offense lies in the same-sex character of the act rather than in its structure as the attempted gang-rape of foreign guests. Susan Niditch (OTL Judges) and Phyllis Trible (*Texts of Terror*) both show that the Genesis 19 / Judges 19 parallel — the outrage at Gibeah, which reworks the same scene-type closely — is built around the violation of guest-right through sexual violence, not around homoerotic desire as such. Claus Westermann's Genesis commentary reads the scene as an assault on the sacred obligation of hospitality, the gravest breach in the ancient Near Eastern social code.

More decisively, when the Hebrew Bible itself looks back at Sodom, it never names same-sex intercourse. Ezekiel 16:49 itemizes Sodom's iniquity: "pride, surfeit of bread, prosperous ease, and she did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy." Walther Zimmerli, in the Hermeneia Ezekiel, takes the list at face value — the indictment is socioeconomic and theological. Verse 50 adds that "they committed *toʿevah* before me," and the apologetic reading routes that *toʿevah* ("abomination") to Leviticus 18:22. But *toʿevah* is a wide-spectrum term — applied to idolatry, dishonest weights, dietary violations, and cultic impropriety — and Zimmerli notes it most naturally caps the catalogue of arrogance just enumerated rather than importing the Levitical sex law. Isaiah 1:10-17 calls the corrupt judges of Judah "rulers of Sodom" precisely because they oppress the widow and orphan; Jeremiah 23:14 likens the lying, adulterous prophets to Sodom. The Hebrew Bible's own cross-references are consistent, and they are about pride, injustice, and social oppression.

The Synoptic Jesus follows that same trajectory: Matthew 10:14-15 and Luke 10:10-12 make Sodom the type-case of inhospitality — the rejection of God's messengers — and Wisdom 19:13-17, written in Greek-speaking Jewish Alexandria, makes it explicit that Sodom "practiced a more bitter hatred of strangers." That is the inherited interpretation through the first century CE.

The shift appears with Jude 7's "strange flesh" (*sarkos heteras*) and the Second Temple para-biblical literature — 1 Enoch 6-11, Jubilees 16, the Testament of Naphtali — where Sodom is read through the Watchers lens of Genesis 6, the illicit crossing between human and angelic kinds. Richard Bauckham, in the Word Biblical Commentary on Jude and 2 Peter, traces this carefully: *sarkos heteras* means "flesh of a different kind," i.e., the Sodomites' (unwitting) attempt to have sexual relations with angels, and possibly the inverse motif of the Watchers' descent — not human same-sex orientation. William Loader's study of sexuality in the pseudepigrapha confirms that the angel-flesh transgression, not homoeroticism per se, drives the Second Temple reading. The further collapse into "homosexuality" as Sodom's defining sin is a later Christian retrojection; John Boswell located its hardening in the medieval West, and Mark Jordan's study of how the very category of "sodomy" was invented in medieval Christian theology traces the moment the city's name was welded to same-sex acts as such.

Whether this is best called a "contradiction" or a layered interpretive trajectory is partly a matter of framing, and the surface tension is real: at least six different sins are named across the texts. But the deeper and more secure point is diachronic. Sodom's sin in the Hebrew Bible and among its first-century inheritors is pride, social oppression, and the violation of hospitality; in the Second Temple apocalyptic tradition it expands to include the forbidden crossing of angel-flesh; the modern "homosexuality" reading is anachronistic and unsupported by the canon's own internal cross-references. Verdict: the multiple sins reflect a genuine and traceable interpretive trajectory, and the single most widely asserted reading — homosexuality — is the least supported by the texts that actually look back on Sodom.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The diverse 'sins of Sodom' are not flatly contradictory but represent a traceable interpretive trajectory: the Hebrew Bible and first-century texts emphasize pride, injustice, and inhospitality; Second Temple literature (behind Jude) adds the angel-flesh transgression; the differing emphases can be read as complementary facets of one narrative tradition. What does NOT harmonize is the popular 'homosexuality' reading, which the canon's own retrospectives on Sodom do not support and which is a later retrojection.

entries.question: Should we look for signs from heaven?
entries.summary: Luke 21:11 has Jesus predict that 'fearful sights and great signs from heaven' will accompany the eschaton, treating such signs as legitimate revelatory markers. Jeremiah 10:2 commands Israel not to be dismayed at the signs of heaven, because that's what the heathen do. One text validates celestial divination as eschatological evidence; the other condemns it as pagan superstition.
entries.commentary:
The Jeremiah 10:2 prohibition is part of an extended anti-idolatry polemic (10:1-16) that critical scholars often associate with Deutero-Jeremianic or post-exilic editorial layers. Robert Carroll in the OTL Jeremiah reads the passage as deliberate exilic-period polemic against Babylonian astral religion — the same celestial-omen practice that produced cuneiform sources like Enūma Anu Enlil. Jack Lundbom in the AB Jeremiah notes that otot ha-shamayim, 'signs of the heavens,' is technical Babylonian astrological vocabulary. The whole point of the verse is to distinguish Israel from its Mesopotamian neighbors by rejecting celestial divination as a religious practice. Don't read the stars, the verse says. That's gentile stuff.

Luke 21:11 is sitting at a completely different cultural moment. The Synoptic Apocalypse is drawing on Jewish apocalyptic traditions in which eschatological cosmic disturbances — earthquakes, eclipses, falling stars, plagues — are read as legitimate revelatory data. Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Luke X-XXIV documents the literary background in Isaiah 13, Joel 2-3, and 1 Enoch, where celestial phenomena announce the day of YHWH. François Bovon in the Hermeneia Luke 3 reads Luke 21:11 as straightforward apocalyptic-tradition material, treating ap' ouranou sēmeia megala — great signs from heaven — as legitimate eschatological markers.

So the contradiction is at a level deeper than 'don't look at the sky' versus 'look at the sky.' It's a contradiction between an anti-divination strand of Israelite religion that wanted to distinguish Yahwistic faith from Babylonian astrology, and an apocalyptic strand that wholeheartedly adopted the same celestial-omen vocabulary because it had become useful for predicting the end times. James VanderKam in *Calendars in the Dead Sea Scrolls* and John Collins in *The Apocalyptic Imagination* both document how Jewish apocalyptic literature (Daniel, 1 Enoch, the Qumran scrolls) is saturated with cosmological signs the Jeremiah author would have considered idolatrous.

The apologist harmonization runs through distinguishing 'taking signs as omens for divinatory purposes' (forbidden) from 'recognizing signs that announce the eschaton' (encouraged). That's a real distinction — and one Christian commentators have made for centuries. But the distinction collapses when you notice that the eschaton-announcing signs in Luke 21 are functionally identical to the divinatory signs in Babylonian astrology: cosmic disturbances read as portents of regime change and divine action. The Lukan apocalypse has imported the technique the Jeremianic anti-idolatry polemic forbade. Take your pick — Jeremiah's anti-astral monotheism, or Luke's apocalyptic-cosmological semiotics.

commentary_out.commentary:
Jeremiah 10:2 sits inside a tightly constructed anti-idolatry polemic (10:1-16) that critical scholars frequently assign to a Deutero-Jeremianic or exilic editorial hand, given its thematic and lexical overlap with Second Isaiah's mockery of idols (Isa 40:18-20; 44:9-20). Robert Carroll, in the Old Testament Library Jeremiah, reads the unit as deliberate exilic-period polemic against Babylonian astral religion — precisely the celestial-omen system that produced the great cuneiform series Enūma Anu Enlil, in which lunar eclipses, planetary motions, and stellar appearances were read as messages from the gods bearing on the fate of kings and nations. Jack Lundbom, in the Anchor Bible Jeremiah, notes that the phrase 'otot ha-shamayim, 'signs of the heavens,' functions as technical vocabulary for exactly this Mesopotamian astrological practice. The verse's force is sociological as much as theological: it is a boundary-marker that distinguishes Israelite Yahwism from the surrounding Mesopotamian cultures by forbidding the reading of the sky for guidance. The prohibition belongs to the same legal-theological stream as Deuteronomy 18:9-14, which lists astrologers, augurs, and diviners among the abominations of the nations Israel must not imitate, and Deuteronomy 4:19, which warns against being 'led astray' to worship the sun, moon, and 'host of heaven.'

Luke 21:11 occupies an entirely different cultural and literary moment. The Synoptic Apocalypse (Mark 13 // Matt 24 // Luke 21) draws on the deep reservoir of Jewish apocalyptic tradition in which eschatological cosmic disturbances — earthquakes, eclipses, falling stars, blood and fire — are read as legitimate revelatory data announcing the Day of YHWH. Joseph Fitzmyer, in the Anchor Bible Luke X-XXIV, traces the literary background through Isaiah 13:10, Joel 2:30-31, and 1 Enoch, where celestial phenomena are the standard furniture of the end. François Bovon, in the Hermeneia Luke commentary, reads the Lukan phrase ap' ouranou sēmeia megala — 'great signs from heaven' — as straightforward apocalyptic-tradition material treating such portents as authentic eschatological markers. John Collins, in The Apocalyptic Imagination, documents at length how Jewish apocalyptic literature (Daniel, 1 Enoch, the Qumran scrolls) is saturated with cosmological signs that the Jeremianic author would have catalogued as Babylonian astrology, and James VanderKam's work on Qumran calendrical and astronomical texts shows how thoroughly Second Temple Judaism had absorbed the very celestial science Jeremiah's polemic rejected. Francesca Rochberg's study of Mesopotamian celestial divination demonstrates that the technical apparatus of reading the heavens as portents passed into the wider ancient world rather than being abolished.

The strongest harmonization, advanced for centuries by Christian commentators, distinguishes two acts: forbidden astral divination, in which one studies the heavens to forecast events and shape decisions (Jeremiah's target), versus passive recognition of God-given signs that accompany the eschaton (Luke's subject). On this reading Jeremiah condemns the diviner's craft, while Luke merely describes phenomena God will send. The distinction is genuine and does dissolve part of the tension: Luke 21 does not counsel anyone to take up horoscopy, and Jeremiah 10 is not denying that God can act in the heavens. The genre gap — legal-paraenetic prohibition versus apocalyptic prediction — reinforces the partial reconciliation. Yet the distinction collapses at the crucial point. The eschaton-announcing signs of Luke 21 are functionally identical to the divinatory signs of Babylonian astrology: cosmic disturbances read as portents of regime change and divine intervention. The Lukan apocalypse has imported the interpretive technique — heavenly events as decodable messages about the fate of nations — that the Jeremianic polemic existed to suppress. The deepest tension is therefore not 'look at the sky' versus 'don't,' but between an anti-divination strand of Israelite religion that defined faithfulness as refusing to read celestial portents, and an apocalyptic strand that wholeheartedly adopted the same celestial-omen semiotics because they had become useful for mapping the end. Verdict: partially harmonizable on genre and act, but the underlying clash between anti-astral monotheism and apocalyptic cosmic semiotics is real.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The two texts operate in different genres and address different acts — Jeremiah forbids astral divination as a religious practice (reading the heavens to predict the future for guidance), while Luke describes celestial phenomena as eschatological accompaniments, not as objects of divinatory inquiry. The distinction is real but only partial, because the apocalyptic signs are functionally the same cosmic portents the anti-divination polemic rejected.

entries.question: Will those who call on the Lord be delivered?
entries.books_in_tension: Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel, Micah, Matthew, Acts, Romans
entries.summary: Joel 2:32 — cited by Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13 — promises that everyone who calls on the name of YHWH/Lord will be saved. Matthew 7:21, Jeremiah 14:12, Ezekiel 8:18, and Micah 3:4 describe categories of people who call on the Lord and are explicitly not heard, not saved, and not delivered. The unconditional Joel-Pauline promise runs into a thicket of conditional and rejection-language texts.
entries.commentary:
Joel 2:32 — kol asher yiqra beshem YHWH yimmalet, 'all who call on the name of YHWH will be delivered' — is one of the most universalist verses in the prophetic corpus. James Crenshaw in the AB Joel reads it as a deliberate expansion of salvation beyond ethnic Israel, prefiguring later inclusivist readings. Paul's two citations of it in Acts 2:21 (Pentecost sermon) and Romans 10:13 (the famous justification-by-faith chapter) lean on the verse's apparent unconditionality: anyone, no qualifications, whoever calls is saved. Doug Moo in the NICNT Romans documents how Romans 10:13 is the climactic prooftext for Paul's argument that the gospel is genuinely universal.

But Matthew 7:21 sees the same vocabulary and explicitly negates it. ou pas ho legon moi kyrie kyrie eiseleusetai eis ten basileian ton ouranon — 'not everyone who says to me Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven.' Dale Allison and W. D. Davies in the ICC Matthew read this as a deliberate intra-Christian polemic: the Matthean community is worried about confessors-without-works, and the verse is designed to deny that 'calling on the Lord' is by itself sufficient. Ulrich Luz in the Hermeneia Matthew 1-7 makes the same point — Matthew 7:21 is anti-charismatic-cheap-grace.

Then the prophetic rejection-texts. Jeremiah 14:12 — when they fast I will not hear their cry — comes from one of the prophet's intercession-prohibition passages discussed in the previous contradiction. Ezekiel 8:18 — though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them — sits inside the temple-vision sequence where YHWH is leaving Jerusalem. Walther Zimmerli in the Hermeneia Ezekiel 1 documents the verse as part of the theological architecture justifying the exile: there comes a point when prayer doesn't work because the divine ear is closed. Micah 3:4 — then they shall cry to YHWH but he will not answer them — is straight prophetic-judgment formula.

The apologist resolution typically distinguishes two senses of 'calling.' Sincere calling with faith and repentance gets you delivered (Joel, Paul). Insincere or merely formal calling without underlying covenant fidelity gets you ignored (Matthew, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Micah). Walter Kaiser and others have run this distinction at length. It's a reasonable systematic-theology move, and it's not wrong. But notice what it costs the universalist reading. Joel 2:32 as cited by Paul in Romans 10 is doing rhetorical work that depends on its unconditionality — kol, pas, everyone. If you have to insert a faith-and-repentance qualifier, you're not citing Joel 2:32 anymore; you're citing 'Joel 2:32 plus the implicit conditions Matthew 7:21 supplies.' That's a synthesis, not a quotation.

The critical reading is the developmental one: Joel's late-prophetic universalism gets taken up by early Christianity as a gospel-of-grace prooftext, while the Matthean and prophetic-judgment strands preserve an older conditional theology in which divine hearing was always contingent on covenant fidelity. Different strata of the canon are working with different theologies of intercessory access. The Bible doesn't speak with one voice on whether prayer-as-such delivers, and the apologetic resolution requires you to read one passage through the implicit assumptions of another.

commentary_out.commentary:
Joel 2:32 (Heb 3:5) — kol asher yiqra' beshem YHWH yimmalet, 'everyone who calls on the name of YHWH will be delivered' — is among the most universalist verses in the prophetic corpus. James Crenshaw, in the Anchor Bible Joel, reads it as a deliberate widening of deliverance and notes the verse's tension with its own immediate context, which restricts the saved to 'the survivors whom YHWH calls' on Mount Zion — so even within Joel the apparent unconditionality is qualified by a remnant theology. Paul cites the verse twice. In Acts 2:21, Luke places it in Peter's Pentecost sermon as the climax of the Joel quotation; in Romans 10:13 Paul makes it the capstone of his argument that Jew and Greek alike are saved by confessing and believing. Douglas Moo, in the New International Commentary Romans, shows how the verse's apparent lack of ethnic and ritual qualification is precisely what makes it serviceable for Paul's universal gospel — but also notes that Paul has just defined 'calling' in 10:9-10 as confession joined to heart-belief, so Paul himself supplies the condition.

Matthew 7:21 takes the same liturgical vocabulary and negates the inference: ou pas ho legōn moi 'Kyrie, Kyrie' eiseleusetai eis tēn basileian tōn ouranōn — 'not everyone who says to me Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father.' W. D. Davies and Dale Allison, in the International Critical Commentary Matthew, read this as intra-Christian polemic: the Matthean community faced confessors-without-works, perhaps charismatic prophets (note 7:22's prophesying and exorcising), and the saying denies that invocation of the Lord's name is by itself sufficient. Ulrich Luz, in the Hermeneia Matthew, concurs, reading 7:21-23 as Matthew's pointed rejection of cheap confession divorced from obedience.

The prophetic rejection-texts supply an older layer. Jeremiah 14:12 belongs to the intercession-prohibition oracles in which YHWH instructs the prophet not to pray for the people and refuses to hear their cry; Lundbom situates it in the drought-and-judgment sequence. Ezekiel 8:18 sits inside the great temple-abomination vision (Ezek 8-11) where YHWH's glory abandons Jerusalem; Walther Zimmerli, in the Hermeneia Ezekiel, reads the closed divine ear as the theological architecture justifying the exile. Micah 3:4 is straight prophetic-judgment form: the corrupt rulers will cry out and YHWH will hide his face. In each, calling on the Lord is explicitly futile.

The strongest harmonization, developed at length by Walter Kaiser and others, distinguishes two senses of 'calling.' Sincere calling joined to faith and repentance secures deliverance (Joel, Acts, Romans); merely formal or hypocritical calling, unaccompanied by covenant fidelity, is justly ignored (Matthew, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Micah). This is a coherent systematic move, and it is exegetically grounded: Matthew 7:21 itself contrasts saying with doing, and Paul defines saving 'calling' as confession-plus-belief. On that reading the texts address different acts under one verb, and the contradiction softens into complementarity. What the harmonization costs, however, is the rhetorical force of the Joel-Pauline citation. Joel 2:32 as deployed in Romans 10 does work that depends on its unqualified pas — everyone, no exceptions — to ground the gospel's reach to Gentiles. If one must import a faith-and-repentance qualifier drawn from Matthew 7:21, one is no longer quoting Joel 2:32 but a synthesis of Joel-plus-Matthew. The critical reading is developmental: Joel's late-prophetic universalism was taken up by early Christianity as a grace prooftext, while the Matthean and prophetic-judgment strands preserved an older conditional theology in which divine hearing was always contingent on covenant fidelity. Different canonical strata operate with different theologies of intercessory access. The systematic reconciliation works, but only by reading each passage through assumptions another passage supplies. Verdict: partially harmonizable as canonical synthesis; not a single unconditional promise.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The texts can be systematically reconciled by distinguishing sincere, repentant calling (delivered: Joel, Acts, Romans) from formal or hypocritical calling unaccompanied by covenant fidelity or obedience (unheard: Matthew, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Micah). The distinction is exegetically defensible but requires reading the unconditional Joel-Pauline 'whoever' through qualifications the other texts supply, so the reconciliation is a canonical synthesis rather than a single coherent voice.
